anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly: The log-file group, buffer, or archiver cannot keep up with redo generation, stalling commits and log switches.
CPU Resource Anomaly: Database processes exhaust available CPU cycles, driving run-queue pressure and system-wide latency.

Composite definition: Both resource layers are saturated at the same time, so every commit must fight for CPU to format and flush redo while the log path itself is already a bottleneck. The engine is therefore constrained by two critical chokepoints on the write path—log throughput and compute capacity.

Combined observable phenomena: 1) commit, log-flush, and log-sync waits climb sharply and remain high; 2) host CPU utilization stays near 100 %, with elevated load average and context-switch rate; 3) the same user transactions appear simultaneously at the top of CPU-time and log-wait lists; 4) checkpoint frequency, log-file switches, or archival backlog accelerates, yet the archiver gets fewer CPU slices to clear segments; 5) latency balloons across both read and write statements, and overall throughput oscillates as scheduler pressure and log-flush pauses alternate; 6) monitoring tools may mis-attribute slowdown to either CPU or I/O alone because both symptoms manifest together.

Causal interaction: Heavy write activity formats redo records, which consumes CPU; once the undersized or mis-placed log subsystem stalls, worker threads spin or block, generating even more context switches and scheduler contention. The CPU saturation, in turn, slows down log-flush and archiver threads, prolonging log-buffer occupancy and amplifying commit back-pressure. This feedback loop escalates quickly: log stall increases wait time per transaction, holding locks and sessions longer, which keeps more processes runnable and pushes CPU even closer to saturation, further delaying log I/O. Without intervention, the mutual reinforcement of compute starvation and log-path congestion can cascade into widespread timeouts, replication lag, or instance freeze.

entry.official_definition: The number of seconds to wait for more data from a connection before aborting the read.
entry.trigger_condition: The server waits for additional data from a connection longer than net_read_timeout.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL server system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
